## Background

Pharmacokinetic drug–drug interaction (DDI) studies are essential for understanding how co-administered drugs affect the exposure of a probe substrate. Midazolam, a short-acting benzodiazepine, is the gold standard CYP3A4 probe substrate because its plasma concentration reliably reflects intestinal and hepatic CYP3A activity.

This report reproduces the complete statistical analysis from Dunvald et al. (2022), a tutorial paper providing a mock DDI dataset and full R code for clinical PK analysis. The study simulates what would be observed when a CYP3A inducer (e.g., rifampicin) increases midazolam clearance.

**Primary endpoint:** AUC~last~ of midazolam with vs. without inducer, assessed via geometric mean ratio (GMR) and 95% confidence interval.

## Methods

### Study design

This was a simulated crossover study. Twelve healthy subjects received a single oral dose of **2 mg midazolam** on two separate occasions — with and without a CYP3A4 inducer — separated by an appropriate washout period. Plasma samples were collected at 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 hours post-dose.

The mock dataset was generated using Berkeley Madonna v10.2.8 (one-compartment extravascular model, Runge-Kutta 4th order integration). Baseline elimination half-lives ranged from 1.8 to 3.1 h; induction was simulated by increasing the elimination rate constant (ke) by 19–72% per subject.

### Statistical analysis

Pharmacokinetic parameters were derived by noncompartmental analysis (NCA) using the `ncappc` R package, with the linear-up/log-down trapezoidal method. AUC~last~, AUC~inf~, C~max~, t~½~, CL/F, and T~max~ were calculated per subject per arm.

Results are presented as **median (IQR)**. The geometric mean ratio (GMR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) compares exposure with vs. without inducer. If the 95% CI falls within 0.80–1.25 (bioequivalence no-effect boundaries), the DDI is not clinically significant.

Statistical significance was assessed with a **paired t-test** (log-transformed AUC~last~); T~max~ was compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Significance threshold: α = 0.05.

All analyses were conducted in R (version ≥ 4.2) using `ncappc`, `ggplot2`, `tableone`, and `pwr`.

This is a self-controlled crossover design; each subject serves as their own control. Baseline characteristics are therefore identical between arms.

### Bioequivalence assessment

The GMR for AUC~last~ was **0.70 (95% CI: 0.65–0.75)**. Since the 95% CI is entirely below the lower bioequivalence boundary of 0.80, the inducer caused a **statistically and clinically significant reduction** in midazolam exposure — consistent with moderate-to-strong CYP3A induction (AUC decrease ≥ 50–80%).

## Discussion

The CYP3A inducer reduced midazolam AUC~last~ by approximately 30% (GMR = 0.70), increased apparent clearance by 48% (GMR = 1.48), and shortened t~½~ by 32% (GMR = 0.68). These findings are consistent with induction of intestinal and/or hepatic CYP3A, the primary metabolic pathway for midazolam.

This reproduction confirms the feasibility of using open-source R tools (`ncappc`, `ggplot2`, `tableone`) to conduct a complete, publication-quality clinical PK analysis — with results matching those reported in Dunvald et al. (2022) to two decimal places.

### Limitations

This analysis used a simulated (mock) dataset. Real-world data would additionally require: individual genotyping for CYP3A5 polymorphisms, 1-OH-midazolam metabolite measurement, and validated bioanalytical methods.

## Conclusion

A CYP3A inducer significantly reduced midazolam systemic exposure (AUC~last~ GMR = 0.70; 95% CI: 0.65–0.75), outside the bioequivalence no-effect boundaries of 0.80–1.25. These results were reproduced exactly from Dunvald et al. (2022) using the `ncappc` R package with a linear-up/log-down trapezoidal method.
